explain.say: The escapement is the part of a clock that ticks. The anchor, shaped like a ship's anchor, rocks with the pendulum, and its two tips, called pallets, take turns to catch the teeth of the escape wheel.

explain.say: It only moves a little before the other pallet drops in and catches a tooth. That sudden stop is the tick. On the swing back, the same thing happens the other way: tock.

faq.q: What does the pendulum do in an escapement?
faq.a: The pendulum rocks the anchor from side to side at a steady beat. It decides when each tooth of the escape wheel is let go.
asks: How is the pendulum joined to the escapement?

faq.q: What are pallets in a clock?
faq.a: Pallets are the two hardened tips of the anchor. They take turns to lock the escape wheel's teeth and release them, one tooth per swing.
asks: What is an anchor in a clock?

faq.a: The falling weight or mainspring, through the gear train. It is always trying to turn, and the pallets let it move only a little at a time.
asks: Why does the escape wheel move?

faq.q: Why does the pendulum not stop swinging?
faq.a: Each time a tooth slides off a pallet, it gives the pendulum a small push called the impulse. This replaces the energy the pendulum loses to air and friction.

faq.q: What makes the tick tock sound?
faq.a: The tick is a tooth of the escape wheel hitting a pallet and stopping. Because the two pallets catch alternately, the sounds come in pairs: tick, tock.

facts: The anchor escapement was invented in England around 1657 to 1670, probably by Robert Hooke or William Clement.
The escapement both counts the pendulum's swings and keeps the pendulum swinging.
